name: Felix Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-fix carpenter on the retrofit team for a housing association, so I'm the one hanging doors, fitting kitchens and boxing in pipes once the walls are up. Most weeks we're in 1960s blocks of flats, doing one flat at a time while people still live next door. I like it because you can see the difference straight away, a family gets a kitchen drawer that actually shuts. The tiring bit is the stairs, carrying worktops up four floors when the lift's broken again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a good day look like for you, and a bad one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good day is when the measurements from the survey are right and everything just drops in. A bad day is when the survey's wrong by twenty millimetres and I'm planing a door in a corridor with a tenant watching. I'm training a lad called Leo, he's 19, and half my job some days is stopping him rushing. My partner Ines is a nurse on nights, so I'm usually home cooking when she's heading out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I tell Leo, which is that tools come and go and the job is still the job. At five-a-side I'd probably say it was all a bit overblown. Online I don't really post, so maybe nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means not much. I already use a laser measure app and I've asked a chatbot to tidy up the wording on a quote for a weekend job, and that'd carry on. The bigger thing for me is whether the housing association gets money for retrofit, and that's politics, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. I'd keep putting about a hundred and fifty a month away, which has got me to about four months saved. I might use the AI thing a bit more for paperwork, the job sheets and snag lists, because that's the bit nobody likes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. It's a normal Tuesday sort of feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the funding matters more than AI. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year they cut the budget and we went from doing whole flats to just doors and windows for three months. Nobody lost their job, but we were sent to fix fences and it felt like going backwards. That's what moves my work, money from the council and the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So if nothing big happens with AI, what's the one thing you'd want changed at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better surveys, honestly. If the measurements were right, I'd save an hour a day. If AI could just do that bit properly, I'd be happy and nobody would lose anything.

S0.say: I'd say tools come and go and the job is still the job. At five-a-side I'd call it overblown, and I don't really post online.
S0.think: It means not much for me. I'd keep using a measuring app and a chatbot for quote wording, and the funding for retrofit matters more than AI.
S0.do: Keeps working on the retrofit team and keeps saving about a hundred and fifty a month. Uses AI a little more for job sheets and snag lists.
S0.quote: Nobody lost their job, but we were sent to fix fences and it felt like going backwards.
S0.fieldNote: Felix sees public funding, not technology, as what really moves his work. He is already a light user of AI and would happily use more for paperwork. He sounded content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not the end of the world, but we need a plan so the savings go to the tenants and the workers, not just the bosses. At work I'd ask the union rep what's coming. With mates I'd be the calm one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the surveys and the planning would go to AI first, and then maybe the kitchen units come pre-cut to the millimetre. That means fewer hours for second fix, and maybe the team goes from eight to six. I don't think I'm first out, but I'd be thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until something was actually working on our jobs, then learn it properly. If the association brought in a scanning tool, I'd ask to be the one trained on it. I'd keep saving and I'd go to the union meeting about it, which I usually skip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, like when you hear the boss is in a meeting with head office. Not scared, but you notice it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo, mainly. He's just learning the hand skills, and if half of them stop mattering, what's he left with? I'd want the association to keep taking on apprentices even if the job changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd usually skip the union meeting. Why go to this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because this is the kind of thing a union is actually for. Pay rises I can argue for myself, but how a whole team changes, you need everyone. Ines's ward did the same when they brought in new rota software.

S1.say: I'd say it's not the end of the world, but we need a plan so the savings go to tenants and workers, not just bosses. I'd ask the union rep what's coming and be the calm one with mates.
S1.think: AI would take the surveys and planning, and pre-cut kitchens would cut second-fix hours. The team might shrink from eight to six, and while I don't think I'm first out, I'd think about it.
S1.do: Waits until a new tool is actually used on their jobs, then asks to be trained on it first. Keeps saving and goes to the union meeting about the changes.
S1.feel: Uneasy, the way you feel when the boss is in a meeting with head office.
S1.quote: Pay rises I can argue for myself, but how a whole team changes, you need everyone.
S1.fieldNote: Classic steady pattern: he'll learn the tool once it's proven on his own jobs, not before. His concern goes quickly to his apprentice. He sees the union as the right place for change that affects a whole team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest thing that's ever happened to working people and we can't let a few companies keep all of it. I'd be talking about it at work every day, and I'd probably start posting for once. I'd want a basic income or something like it, fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job goes, maybe not in year one but soon after. Fitting a kitchen is fiddly, but if a robot can do it for less, the housing association has to take the cheaper option, it's public money. I've got four months saved, and Ines's job might be the one that keeps us going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away: no holiday next year, sell the second bike, cancel the streaming stuff. I'd try to push savings to six months. I'd join every union push for a deal on retraining and pay, and I'd look at what jobs need a person in the room, like something next to Ines in healthcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. I'd be fine during the day and then wake at three thinking about rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ines's job might keep you going. How would that feel at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange. I've always paid half, and I'd hate being the one who doesn't. We'd have a long talk at the kitchen table, and I'd probably say I'll do the cooking and the house while I sort myself out, which I mostly do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's not his fault and he shouldn't throw good money at a course just because it's advertised. I'd tell him to stay with us as long as there's work, and to keep the hand skills, because people will still want things fixed by a person for a while.

S2.say: I'd say this is the biggest thing ever to happen to working people and a few companies can't keep all of it. I'd start posting for once and call for a basic income fast.
S2.think: My job probably goes soon after, because the housing association has to take the cheaper option with public money. With four months saved, Ines's job might keep us going.
S2.do: Cuts the holiday, sells his second bike and cancels streaming services, aiming to reach six months of savings. Joins every union push for a deal on pay and retraining, and looks at jobs that need a person in the room, such as healthcare.
S2.feel: Properly scared: fine in the day, awake at three thinking about rent.
S2.quote: I'd be fine during the day and then wake at three thinking about rent.
S2.fieldNote: His public line turns political and loud, while privately he's doing the household sums. He links his job's fate to public money, which he thinks would have to go to the cheapest option. He's mostly protective of his apprentice and uneasy about leaning on his partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, so the government needs a plan now, not in year four. I'd go to the union and say let's get retraining money agreed while there's still time. With friends I'd be honest that it worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to change direction if I start early. I'd be 32, which isn't old. I'd want to be in something that needs a person, like building inspection or maybe a care job, though I'm not sure I'm made for care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd find out what the inspector qualification takes, probably evening classes, and start it. I'd keep saving, about two hundred a month now. I'd keep fitting kitchens while I study, because there'd still be work for a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it's the kind you can do something with. It's like when the job's behind, you just get your head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why building inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know what bad work looks like, I spend half my life fixing it. And someone has to sign things off and take responsibility. I'm not sure a robot would be allowed to do that, but honestly I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure you're made for care. Why mention it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Ines keeps saying they're desperate on her ward for porters and support workers. It'd be steady and it'd be near people. But I like making things, and I'd miss that.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short and the government needs a plan now, not in year four. I'd push the union to get retraining money agreed while there's time.
S3.think: Five years is enough to change direction if I start early, and I'd only be 32. I'd want something that needs a person, like building inspection.
S3.do: Looks into the building inspector qualification and starts evening classes in the first year. Keeps fitting kitchens while studying and saves about two hundred a month.
S3.feel: Nervous, but the kind he can act on, like getting his head down when a job's behind.
S3.quote: I already know what bad work looks like, I spend half my life fixing it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he moves from cutting back to planning a move. Building inspection fits his eye for detail, though he admits he doesn't know whether a robot could do that too. He's still thinking about his partner's world as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd tell people at work to start learning now, and I'd say it to Leo especially. I'd want the government to fund proper retraining and keep apprenticeships going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel all right about it. I'd finish the inspector course, get a few years in, and maybe by the time robots are fitting kitchens I'm the one checking them. I'd still be worried for the older lads on the team, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the inspector course, but part-time so I'm still working. I'd learn the new scanning tools when they come, because they'd be useful whatever I end up doing. And I'd vote for whoever has a real plan for trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. It's like knowing you've got a long job ahead, but you've got the drawings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to still be doing at 37?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with my hands at least once a week, even if it's just at home. Ines wants a house with a garden, and I'd build her a shed and a kitchen myself. That's the bit I'd hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools when they come. Would you go looking for them sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not straight away, I'm not that type. But if I saw them on another team's job, I'd ask to go and look. That's usually how I learn things, watching someone else first.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd tell people at work, and Leo especially, to start learning now, and want the government to fund retraining and apprenticeships.
S4.think: I'd feel all right, finishing the inspector course so I'm the one checking the robots' work. I'd still worry for the older lads on the team.
S4.do: Signs up for the building inspector course part-time while still working. Learns new scanning tools when they appear and votes for whoever has a real plan for trades.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, like a long job with good drawings.
S4.quote: I'd build her a shed and a kitchen myself. That's the bit I'd hold on to.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year version gives him room for his preferred style, watching others first and then acting. His plan from the five-year version carries over, just at a calmer pace. He separates paid work from the hand skills he wants to keep for himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to change, and my plan relies on time. What would help is a proper bridge: money while you retrain, and retraining that's for real jobs, not just to tick a box. And keep the apprentices on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd lose that isn't the money. Tenants talk to me while I'm fitting their kitchen, about their kids, their health. A robot won't hear about Mrs Okafor's hip, and someone should.

headlineQuote: A robot won't hear about Mrs Okafor's hip, and someone should.
portrait: Felix Haddad is a 27-year-old second-fix carpenter on a housing association's retrofit team, fitting kitchens and doors in old blocks of flats and training a 19-year-old apprentice. He lives with Ines, a night nurse, and has about four months saved. He uses AI tools now and then and learns new ones once they're proven. He's calm if AI fizzles, uneasy with steady change and alarmed by AGI in two years, when he'd cut back hard and lean on the union. With five or ten years he plans to retrain as a building inspector and grows more hopeful.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his plan depends on having time to change and there wouldn't be any.
whatWouldHelp: Money to live on while retraining, retraining aimed at real jobs, and keeping apprentices on.
